newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Sept 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Sept 25.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- NATWEST IN 5 BILLION DOLLAR LOANS SWITCH

National Westminster Bank is expected to announce on Wednesday a landmark securities plan involving the removal of 5 billion dollars (3.02 billion stg) of corporate loans from its balance sheet by converting them into securities to be sold to international investors.
-- INSTITUTIONS PRESS FOR ALL DIRECTORS TO FACE RE-ELECTION

The investment committee of the National Association of Pension Funds, the UK's leading institutional investor group, has written to the country's 300 largest public companies urging them to put all their directors up regularly for re-election by shareholders. The move follows concern among institutional investor's about their inability to vote on poorly performing directors.
-- CURRENT ACCOUNT SURPLUS RISES TO NINE-YEAR HIGH

The Chancellor Kenneth Clarke received a timely economic boost on Tuesday after figures revealed the UK recorded the biggest current account surplus for nine years, after record income from investment and services in the second quarter. The UK's current account surplus, adjusted for seasonal factors, was 457 million stg for the second quarter, compared to a deficit of 786 million stg in the first quarter.
-- BELGIAN FERRY LINE TO CLOSE AS TUNNEL COMPETITION BITES

Belgian state-owned ferry company Regie voor maritem Transport (RMT) is to cut up to 1,300 jobs over the next three years as it winds down its cross-Channel operations. The job losses are seen as the first casualties of competition from the Channel tunnel, and have prompted Sally Ferries, RMT's partner on Ramsgate-Ostend services, to establish a tie up with Australian high speed ferry operator Holyman.
-- EU ACTS TO UNBLOCK DEAL ON IT

The European Union has moved to clear the way for December's ministerial conference of the World Trade Organization to reach agreement on liberalising world trade in information technology products. The EU had been blocking a deal by insisting that European semiconductor manufacturers be allowed to join an industry body set up by Japanese and US chipmakers, but the US wanted the EU to scrap its semiconductor tariffs before joining. Now EU trade commissioner Sir Leon Brittan has offered a compromise on entry.
-- DIRECTORS CALL FOR CURBS ON SPENDING

The Institute of Directors, the body which represents Britain's employers, has urged the Chancellor to cut government expenditure in the Autumn budget, but not taxes. The IOD said that reducing public borrowing, which it described as a 'blot on Britain's economic performance', should be the chancellor's priority.
-- MOD HOMES BUYER DROPS RELOCATION CLAUSE

The Japanese-led consortium which is paying 1.6 billion stg for the married quarters housing of the Ministry of Defence has dropped a controversial option allowing it to move service families to new sites. The consortium, Annington House, is majority owned by Japanese securities house Nomura. It wanted to use the 'site exchange' option to relocate service communities so it could redevelop the former MOD sites.
-- AT&T WARNS ON LONG-DISTANCE PHONE BUSINESS

U.S. telecommunications giant AT&T has issued a warning about the performance of its core long-distance telephone business, after a marketing war in the U.S. on long-distance business, and following the costs of developing new Internet access and other services. Shares in AT&T on Wall Street fell $5 3/8 to $51 7/8 following the warning, the second time this year that AT&T stock has plunged sharply. In July shares fell when the company said it was losing market share to other carriers.
-- AEA TO GET FINAL FLOATATION PRICING TODAY

The final price for the floatation of AEA Technology, the engineering and science group spun off from the UK Atomic Energy Authority, will be announced by the government on Wednesday. The final figure is expected to be within the new, raised indicative range of 250p to 280p.
-- LUCAS VARITY PLANS COST-CUTTING

Anglo-US automotive and aerospace components group LucasVarity is said to be considering a five-year business plan which would involve heavy cost-cutting. The board is due to meet Thursday, when it will be told that special management teams have been established to identify large savings following the merger earlier this month of Britain's Lucas Industries with Varity Corporation of the US.
